how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect CI/CD pipeline configuration files (Ansible playbooks, Terraform configs, Kubernetes manifests) to verify whether a patching or image-update workflow references the load balancer component.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more playbook or pipeline files referencing the load balancer with patch or upgrade tasks indicates a defined cadence. No matching files suggests ad hoc patching only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the system owner or operations team to confirm whether a written patching policy document exists that explicitly covers network infrastructure components including load balancers, with a defined frequency.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Security policy repository or GRC tool (e.g., Confluence, SharePoint) → Patch Management Policy
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A policy document specifying patch frequency (e.g., 'critical patches within 30 days, standard patches within 90 days') that explicitly includes load balancers confirms true. No document or exclusion of infrastructure components sets this to false.

typical_values: true (enterprises with mature ITSM and defined patch windows, or DevOps environments with automated image rebuilds)
false (small teams relying on manual, unscheduled patching or where patch policy covers only endpoint/server OS but not network appliances)

option_description: Records the number of days elapsed since the load balancer software was last updated to a version that addressed known security vulnerabilities. This is a continuous measure used alongside patching cadence to determine whether the software is effectively maintained.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Unpatched Load Balancer Software' when patching_cadence_defined is false AND days_since_last_patch exceeds 90. A high value (>90 days without a defined cadence) indicates the load balancer is operating in a prolonged unpatched state, increasing the probability that disclosed CVEs (T1190, T1210) are present and exploitable. Even with a defined cadence, large values indicate cadence is not being followed. This metric provides evidence for compliance reporting against PCI-DSS Requirement 6 and CIS Control 7.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the installation timestamp of the load balancer package using the package manager to calculate days since last update.
how_to_obtain.command: rpm -q --queryformat '%{INSTALLTIME:date}\n' haproxy nginx 2>/dev/null; dpkg-query -W -f='${Package} ${Version} ${db:Status-Status}\n' haproxy nginx 2>/dev/null; stat -c '%y' $(which haproxy nginx 2>/dev/null | head -1)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns a timestamp such as 'Mon 15 Jan 2024 10:23:45'. Calculate the difference between this date and today's date in days. The result is the value for this attribute.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the package manager history log to find the most recent upgrade event for the load balancer package.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -i 'haproxy\|nginx\|traefik' /var/log/dpkg.log 2>/dev/null | grep ' install\| upgrade' | tail -5; grep -i 'haproxy\|nginx\|traefik' /var/log/dnf.log /var/log/yum.log 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'installed\|updated' | tail -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries with timestamps showing the last upgrade event, e.g., '2024-01-15 10:23:45 upgrade haproxy 2.6.12 2.6.14'. Use the most recent entry date to calculate days elapsed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review change management records or deployment pipeline logs for the last production deployment of the load balancer configuration or binary.
how_to_obtain.command: ls -lt /etc/haproxy/ /etc/nginx/ | head -20; find /var/lib/dpkg/info -name 'haproxy.*' -o -name 'nginx.*' 2>/dev/null | xargs stat -c '%y %n' 2>/dev/null | sort -r | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: File modification timestamps on package info files reflect the last package installation/upgrade. The most recent modification date gives the baseline for calculating days elapsed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the CI/CD pipeline or infrastructure-as-code deployment history (e.g., Terraform state, Ansible AWX job history, Kubernetes deployment history) for the last successful load balancer image or package update.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl rollout history deployment/nginx-ingress-controller -n ingress-nginx 2>/dev/null; helm history nginx-ingress 2>/dev/null | tail -5
how_to_obtain.navigation: CI/CD platform (Jenkins, GitLab CI, GitHub Actions) → Pipeline runs → Filter by load balancer deployment job → Last successful run date
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A deployment record with a timestamp. Subtract this date from today to obtain the integer value for days_since_last_patch.

typical_values: 0–30 (actively maintained environments with automated patching or monthly patch windows)
31–90 (quarterly patching cadence, still within typical compliance thresholds)
91–365 (policy gap or forgotten infrastructure — triggers exposure in Rego when cadence is undefined)

option_description: Specifies whether multi-factor authentication is actively required for all administrative logins to the load balancer management interface, including web console, REST API, SSH access, and CLI. A value of true means no admin session can be established with a single authentication factor.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'Missing Multi Factor Authentication On Admin' when mfa_enforced_on_admin_interface is not true (falsy), and also references this attribute in the 'Default Or Weak Admin Credentials' rule. Without MFA, stolen or guessed credentials are sufficient for full administrative compromise (T1110.004 credential stuffing, T1078.001 default accounts). Because the load balancer controls traffic routing and TLS termination, admin access enables traffic interception, backend pool manipulation, and certificate theft. MFA is the primary control preventing credential-based administrative takeover.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the HAProxy runtime API authentication config and NGINX Plus management authentication settings for MFA integration references.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of MFA-related configuration directives (e.g., RADIUS server address with MFA, TACACS+ integration) confirms a mechanism exists. Absence suggests MFA is not configured at the load balancer level and may rely on upstream IdP or OS PAM.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check PAM configuration for SSH and management services on the load balancer host to determine if MFA is enforced at the OS level.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: PAM entries referencing MFA modules (pam_duo, pam_google_authenticator) and sshd AuthenticationMethods showing 'publickey,keyboard-interactive' indicate MFA is enforced for SSH. Absence means SSH admin access may be single-factor.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log in to the load balancer vendor web management interface and navigate to the authentication or user management settings to verify MFA requirement.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Load balancer web console → Settings/Administration → Authentication → MFA/Two-Factor Authentication → Verify 'Enforce MFA for all admin users' is enabled
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A toggle or policy setting showing MFA enforcement is 'Enabled' or 'Required' for all administrative roles. 'Disabled' or 'Optional' sets this attribute to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the Identity Provider (IdP) configuration for SAML SSO or RADIUS/TACACS+ integration to confirm MFA is mandated in the authentication policy applied to load balancer admin access.
how_to_obtain.navigation: IdP console (Okta, Azure AD, Duo) → Applications → Load Balancer Admin App → Sign-On Policy → Verify MFA is required for the admin user group
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An active MFA policy requiring a second factor (TOTP, push, hardware token) for the user group assigned administrative access to the load balancer confirms true.

typical_values: false (most default configurations rely solely on local username/password)
true (environments with Duo, Okta, Azure AD Conditional Access, or hardware tokens enforced)

option_description: Identifies the specific authentication mechanism configured for the load balancer management interface. This enum captures the full authentication method including whether it inherently includes MFA (e.g., saml_sso_with_mfa, radius_with_mfa, tacacs_with_mfa) or uses credentials-only approaches (local_password, ldap_no_mfa, radius_no_mfa) or certificate-based authentication.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Missing Multi Factor Authentication On Admin' when admin_auth_method is in ['local_password', 'ldap_no_mfa', 'radius_no_mfa']. These methods provide no second factor, making credential theft (T1110.004, T1078.001) sufficient for administrative takeover. local_password is the highest-risk option as it relies entirely on a locally managed secret with no centralized policy enforcement. certificate_based provides strong authentication without requiring a traditional second factor. Methods with embedded MFA (saml_sso_with_mfa, radius_with_mfa, tacacs_with_mfa) satisfy the Rego policy requirement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect load balancer configuration files for authentication backend directives to identify the configured method.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HAProxy 'userlist' blocks with 'user' entries indicate local_password. LDAP server references indicate ldap_no_mfa or ldap_with_mfa. RADIUS server directives indicate radius_no_mfa or radius_with_mfa depending on server configuration. ssl_client_certificate indicates certificate_based.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Traefik, examine the traefik.yml or static configuration for authentication middleware definitions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: basicAuth indicates local_password. forwardAuth pointing to an external IdP may indicate saml_sso_with_mfa if the IdP enforces MFA. tls.options with clientAuth.caFiles indicates certificate_based.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the authentication configuration section of the load balancer web management console to view the configured authentication provider.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Load balancer web console → Administration → Authentication Settings → Authentication Method dropdown — note the selected value and any MFA checkbox state
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The UI should display the current authentication method (e.g., 'RADIUS', 'LDAP', 'Local Database', 'SAML 2.0'). Map this to the enum values: RADIUS without MFA server-side policy = radius_no_mfa; SAML with IdP MFA policy = saml_sso_with_mfa.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check PAM service configuration for the management interface service to identify the authentication stack.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: PAM modules reveal the authentication method: pam_unix.so = local_password; pam_ldap.so without MFA module = ldap_no_mfa; pam_radius_auth.so = radius_no_mfa or radius_with_mfa; pam_duo.so or pam_google_authenticator.so alongside another module = method_with_mfa.

typical_values: local_password (default for most software load balancers, highest risk)
ldap_no_mfa (common in enterprise environments integrated with Active Directory but without MFA)
radius_with_mfa (common in environments using Cisco ISE or FreeRADIUS with Duo)
certificate_based (common in PKI-mature environments and mutual TLS management access)
saml_sso_with_mfa (modern cloud-native deployments using Okta or Azure AD)

option_description: Specifies the number of seconds of inactivity after which the load balancer automatically terminates an authenticated administrative or management session. A value of 0 means no inactivity timeout is configured and sessions persist indefinitely until explicitly logged out.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'No Session Timeout On Management Session' when management_session_timeout_seconds equals 0. Indefinitely persistent sessions expose the load balancer to session hijacking (T1563), stolen session cookie reuse (T1539, T1550.004), and unauthorized access from unattended terminals. An authenticated session without expiry means a compromised session token provides permanent administrative access. Recommended values range from 300 seconds (5 minutes) for high-security environments to 900 seconds (15 minutes) for standard operations, with 1800 seconds (30 minutes) as a common maximum for usability balance.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search HAProxy configuration for timeout settings applicable to the stats or admin socket interface.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HAProxy uses directives such as 'timeout http-keep-alive', 'timeout http-request', 'timeout client'. For the stats page: 'stats timeout' value. A value of 0 or absence of a session timeout directive for management access means management_session_timeout_seconds = 0.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check NGINX management or stub_status module configuration for session timeout settings, and review any Lua-based session management.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Values shown in seconds for timeout directives. Note that NGINX Plus dashboard may have separate session management. keepalive_timeout value represents connection persistence. Absent session expiry settings for admin access means value = 0.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For F5 BIG-IP or similar enterprise load balancers, query the management session timeout via tmsh or REST API.
how_to_obtain.command: tmsh list sys httpd auth-pam-idle-timeout 2>/dev/null; curl -sk -u admin:password https://localhost/mgmt/tm/sys/httpd 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool | grep -i 'idle\|timeout\|session'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output such as 'auth-pam-idle-timeout 1200' indicates a 1200-second (20-minute) timeout is configured. A value of 0 or 'indefinite' confirms management_session_timeout_seconds = 0.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the session management settings in the load balancer web console to read the configured inactivity timeout value.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Load balancer web console → System → Management → Session Settings → Idle Timeout or Session Timeout field — record the value in seconds
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numeric value in seconds (e.g., 900, 1800) or a field showing 'No Timeout' / 0. Record this exact integer value as management_session_timeout_seconds.

typical_values: 0 (default in many appliances and software load balancers — no timeout configured)
300 (5 minutes — high-security or PCI-DSS compliant environments)
900 (15 minutes — CIS benchmark recommendation for management interfaces)
1800 (30 minutes — common enterprise compromise between security and usability)
3600 (1 hour — less secure but common in operational environments with persistent monitoring)

option_description: A boolean flag indicating whether the session inactivity timeout mechanism is explicitly enabled and actively applied to management console sessions. This is distinct from the timeout duration value itself — a system may have a non-zero timeout value configured but the enforcement mechanism may be disabled via a separate toggle or missing configuration directive.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'No Session Timeout On Management Session' when session_timeout_enforced is not true (falsy), independent of the management_session_timeout_seconds value. This means a load balancer can have a timeout value set but still be vulnerable if enforcement is not enabled. Unenforced sessions enable session hijacking (T1563), persistent use of stolen session cookies (T1539, T1550.004), and unauthorized reuse on shared terminals or jump hosts. This attribute captures the enforcement state separately because some platforms require an explicit 'enable' flag in addition to the numeric timeout value.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search load balancer configuration files for explicit session timeout enablement directives separate from the duration value.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of an explicit enablement directive set to true, 'on', or 'yes' confirms session_timeout_enforced = true. If only a numeric value exists without an enable flag, verify platform documentation to determine if the value alone activates enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For F5 BIG-IP, verify that the management idle timeout is not set to 'indefinite' and that the PAM configuration is active.
how_to_obtain.command: tmsh list sys httpd auth-pam-idle-timeout auth-pam-validate-ip 2>/dev/null; tmsh show sys httpd 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'timeout'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'auth-pam-idle-timeout 900' (non-zero value) with no 'indefinite' keyword confirms enforcement is active. 'auth-pam-idle-timeout 0' or 'indefinite' means enforcement is disabled, setting this to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the load balancer management web console and verify there is an explicit 'Enable Session Timeout' or 'Enforce Idle Timeout' toggle that is set to the active/enabled state.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Load balancer web console → System → Management → Session Settings → Locate 'Enable Session Timeout' or 'Enforce Idle Timeout' toggle → Confirm it is set to 'On' or 'Enabled'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An 'Enabled' or 'Active' state for the session timeout enforcement toggle confirms true. 'Disabled' or absence of the setting entirely (relying only on the numeric value) sets this to false pending platform documentation review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify enforcement by testing an actual management session: authenticate, leave idle for a duration less than the configured timeout, then attempt to use the session; also verify the session is terminated after the configured timeout elapses.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 401 Unauthorized or session-expired response after the timeout period confirms enforcement is active (true). A successful response with valid data after the timeout period confirms enforcement is not working (false).

typical_values: false (common default on many platforms where timeout value exists in config but enforcement requires a separate enable flag that is not set)
true (explicitly configured on hardened systems where both the timeout duration and enforcement mechanism are active)

option_description: Controls whether the load balancer's service discovery integration (Consul, Kubernetes API, etcd) requires valid authentication credentials—tokens, certificates, or mTLS—before accepting backend node registrations from the discovery service.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the `backend_pool_auto_discovery_without_authentication` exposure whenever `discovery_service_auth_enabled` is false. An unauthenticated discovery channel allows any host that can reach the discovery service to inject arbitrary backend nodes into the active pool, enabling traffic hijacking and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. This is rated high criticality (score 8) and maps to T1046 (Network Service Discovery) and T1580 (Cloud Infrastructure Discovery).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Consul-backed load balancers, inspect the agent configuration for an ACL token or verify the Consul agent token is set in the load balancer's environment.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows a non-empty ACL token value or references to token files; absence of any token indicates auth is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the load balancer's service discovery configuration block for credential references. For HAProxy with Consul, check the dataplaneapi or consul-template config. For NGINX Plus, inspect the zone_sync or upstream resolver block.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'token', 'ca_file', 'cert_file', 'tls_config', or 'credentials' directives in the discovery stanza indicates authentication is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API or Consul HTTP API without credentials to test whether unauthenticated access is permitted, which would indicate auth is not enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 401 or 403 HTTP response confirms authentication is required. A 200 response with data confirms authentication is NOT enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform or infrastructure team to confirm whether the load balancer service account or configuration management pipeline injects discovery credentials at deploy time, and review the CI/CD pipeline secrets configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation or pipeline scripts show a secrets injection step that populates a Consul token, Kubernetes service account token, or etcd client certificate before the load balancer process starts.

option_description: Controls whether the load balancer validates newly discovered or dynamically registered backend nodes—via allowlist membership, cryptographic signature verification, or an approval workflow—before adding them to the active backend pool.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `backend_pool_auto_discovery_without_authentication` when `backend_node_registration_validation_enabled` is false even if `discovery_service_auth_enabled` is true. Without node validation, a compromised internal host or a stolen discovery credential can register a rogue backend and intercept production traffic. This is rated high criticality (score 8) and maps to T1046 and T1580.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search the load balancer configuration for allowlist, whitelist, or node-filter directives. In Traefik, look for `constraints` or `tags` filters in provider configuration. In Consul-template-generated HAProxy config, check for node tag requirements.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of tag constraints, IP allowlists, or certificate validation directives indicates validation is enabled. Empty result or pure auto-accept configuration indicates it is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to register a test backend node via the discovery API (using valid credentials if auth is enabled) without it appearing on any known allowlist. Check if it is added to the active pool.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If the test node appears immediately in the load balancer's backend pool without any approval step, validation is NOT enabled. A rejection or absence from the pool confirms validation is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In cloud-managed load balancers (AWS ALB/NLB, GCP Load Balancing, Azure Application Gateway), navigate to the backend pool or target group configuration and verify that membership is defined by explicit target registration or allowlisted instance tags rather than fully open auto-discovery.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → EC2 → Load Balancers → [LB Name] → Target Groups → [Group Name] → Targets tab; verify targets are registered explicitly or filtered by specific tags.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Target registration shows explicit member IDs or tag-filter rules. An 'Auto-scaling group' attachment without tag filtering indicates insufficient validation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the infrastructure-as-code (Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation) that defines backend pool membership to confirm that registration is controlled by explicit resource references or tag selectors rather than open service discovery.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: IaC code references explicit resource IDs or restrictive tag selectors for backend membership. Open discovery with no filter criteria indicates validation is absent.

option_description: Controls whether automated alerting is configured to notify operators when TLS certificates on client-facing listeners or backend listeners are approaching their expiration date.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `missing_certificate_validity_monitoring` when `certificate_expiry_alerting_enabled` is false. Without expiry alerts, certificates silently expire, causing service outages or forcing operators to continue running the load balancer with expired, untrusted certificates—opening the door to T1649 (Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates) and T1587.003 (Digital Certificates). The exposure is rated low criticality (score 2) but can cascade to service-level incidents.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the load balancer host or monitoring agent configuration for certificate expiry check scripts, cron jobs, or alerting integrations.
how_to_obtain.command: crontab -l 2>/dev/null | grep -i cert; ls /etc/cron.d/ /etc/cron.daily/ | grep -i cert; systemctl list-units --type=timer | grep -i cert
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of a cron job, systemd timer, or scheduled task referencing certificate checking indicates alerting may be configured. Absence suggests it is not.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect SIEM, Prometheus, Datadog, or Nagios/Icinga configuration for certificate expiry alert rules targeting the load balancer's listeners.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Alert rules referencing certificate expiry thresholds against the load balancer's FQDN or IP confirm alerting is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In cloud-managed environments, check the certificate manager for expiry notification settings. In AWS ACM, verify SNS notifications for expiry are configured. In GCP, check Cloud Monitoring alert policies for certificate expiry.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → Certificate Manager → [Certificate] → check 'Renewal Status' and SNS topic for expiry events; GCP Console → Monitoring → Alerting → check for 'ssl_certificate/days_until_expiration' metric alert.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An active SNS topic subscription or monitoring alert policy targeting certificate expiry confirms alerting is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Ask the operations team to demonstrate or show documentation of the last certificate expiry alert received and the notification channel (email, PagerDuty, Slack) it used.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Team can show a historical alert notification with certificate name, expiry date, and notification timestamp. Inability to produce this indicates alerting is absent or untested.

option_description: Controls whether an automated mechanism—such as cert-manager, AWS ACM auto-renewal, HashiCorp Vault PKI, or a CI/CD pipeline—renews and rotates TLS certificates before expiry across all load balancer listeners.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `missing_certificate_validity_monitoring` when both `automated_certificate_rotation_enabled` and `certificate_expiry_alerting_enabled` are false. Automated rotation eliminates the manual renewal window during which expired certificates cause service outages or force insecure workarounds. Without it, adversaries can exploit expiry windows to introduce forged certificates (T1649) or intercept traffic during certificate re-issuance delays.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for cert-manager CRDs in Kubernetes, ACME client configuration, or Vault agent sidecar configuration on the load balancer.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get certificate,certificaterequest,clusterissuer -A 2>/dev/null; ls /etc/letsencrypt/renewal/ 2>/dev/null; vault lease lookup <certificate-lease-id> 2>/dev/null; systemctl status certbot.timer 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active cert-manager Certificate resources, certbot renewal timer, or Vault lease entries confirm automated rotation is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the load balancer and certificate management configuration files for ACME, Vault PKI, or secrets manager renewal references.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACME provider blocks, Vault PKI role references, or cert-manager annotations confirm automated rotation is in place.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS ACM for managed renewal status on certificates attached to the load balancer, or query cert-manager API for certificate conditions.
how_to_obtain.command: aws acm list-certificates --query 'CertificateSummaryList[*].[CertificateArn,RenewalEligibility]' --output table; kubectl get certificate -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.status.conditions[*].type}{"\n"}{end}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACM shows 'ELIGIBLE' for managed renewal; cert-manager shows 'Ready=True' condition. 'INELIGIBLE' or absent conditions indicate manual rotation only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In cloud console, verify the certificate attached to the load balancer listener shows auto-renewal status.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → Certificate Manager → [Certificate ARN] → Renewal tab → confirm 'Pending automatic renewal' or 'Renewed'; Azure Portal → App Service Certificates → [Cert] → Auto Renew = On.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Auto-renewal status shows 'Enabled' or 'Pending automatic renewal'. 'Disabled' or no renewal status indicates automated rotation is not configured.

option_description: Specifies the number of days before a TLS certificate expires at which the alerting system is configured to fire a notification. A value of 0 means no threshold is defined, meaning no advance warning will be issued.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `missing_certificate_validity_monitoring` when `certificate_expiry_alerting_enabled` is true but `minimum_days_before_expiry_alert` equals 0—indicating alerting is nominally enabled but effectively useless with no threshold. Industry best practice requires at least a 30-day lead time to allow for certificate procurement, change management, and deployment. Too short a window risks undetected expiry, enabling T1649 attack scenarios and service outages.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Prometheus alerting rules or Nagios/Icinga check commands for the certificate expiry threshold value configured for the load balancer endpoints.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Alert rule shows a 'for' duration or threshold value such as '30d', '720h', or '--days 30'. A value of 0 or absent threshold indicates no warning window is set.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If using a custom certificate monitoring script (e.g., check_ssl_cert, ssl-cert-check), inspect its invocation parameters for the warning/critical day thresholds.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Script invocation shows '-w 30 -c 14' or equivalent warning/critical threshold parameters. Missing parameters indicate threshold is 0 or undefined.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the monitoring platform API (Prometheus, Datadog, PagerDuty) for alert rules targeting certificate expiry on load balancer endpoints and extract the threshold value.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/rules | python3 -m json.tool | grep -A5 -i 'cert\|expir\|ssl'; curl -s -H 'DD-API-KEY: <key>' 'https://api.datadoghq.com/api/v1/monitor' | python3 -m json.tool | grep -A10 'ssl_certificate'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Alert rule JSON shows a threshold expression such as 'ssl_earliest_cert_expiry - time() < 86400 * 30'. A missing or zero-valued threshold confirms the gap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In cloud monitoring or SIEM dashboards, navigate to certificate monitoring alerts and inspect the configured expiry notification window.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → CloudWatch → Alarms → search for 'DaysToExpiry'; GCP Console → Monitoring → Alerting → find policy for 'ssl_certificate/days_until_expiration' and check threshold value.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Alert policy threshold shows a positive integer (e.g., 30 days). A threshold of 0 or no alert policy confirms the minimum days value is 0.

option_description: Controls whether ICMP traffic (ping, traceroute, timestamp, etc.) is permitted on the load balancer's external or management interfaces without source IP restriction, allowing any host to probe the load balancer's reachability and internal network topology.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `unrestricted_icmp_and_diagnostic_protocols` when `icmp_unrestricted` is true. Unrestricted ICMP enables adversary reconnaissance via ping sweeps and traceroute to map internal network topology (T1016 - System Network Configuration Discovery) and can be abused as a covert non-application layer protocol channel (T1095). While rated low criticality (score 2), it meaningfully increases attacker situational awareness of the environment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect host-level firewall rules (iptables, nftables, ufw) for ICMP accept rules and their source restrictions.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v | grep -i icmp; ip6tables -L INPUT -n -v | grep -i icmp; nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null | grep -i icmp; ufw status verbose 2>/dev/null | grep -i icmp
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An ICMP ACCEPT rule with source 0.0.0.0/0 confirms unrestricted ICMP. Rules restricted to specific source CIDRs or a DROP/REJECT default indicate ICMP is restricted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send ICMP echo requests to the load balancer's public IP from an external test host to determine if ping is permitted.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Successful ping replies from external host confirm ICMP is unrestricted. 100% packet loss or 'Request timeout' indicates ICMP is blocked or restricted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review cloud security group or network ACL rules for ICMP permissions on the load balancer's interface.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids <sg-id> --query 'SecurityGroups[*].IpPermissions[?IpProtocol==`icmp`]' --output json; gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter='allowed.IPProtocol=icmp' --format=json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ICMP rule with CidrIp 0.0.0.0/0 confirms unrestricted inbound ICMP. Absence of ICMP rules or restricted source CIDRs indicates it is controlled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In cloud console, navigate to the security group or firewall rules for the load balancer and check for any ICMP ingress rules and their source IP ranges.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → EC2 → Security Groups → [LB Security Group] → Inbound Rules → filter by Type: 'All ICMP - IPv4'; Azure Portal → Network Security Groups → [NSG] → Inbound Security Rules → filter by Protocol: ICMP.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ICMP rule with source 0.0.0.0/0 or Any = unrestricted (true). No ICMP rule or source-restricted ICMP = restricted (false).

option_description: Controls whether the SNMP agent is running and listening on the load balancer host for monitoring or management purposes. When enabled without source restriction or with weak community strings, SNMP exposes detailed infrastructure configuration data.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `unrestricted_icmp_and_diagnostic_protocols` when `snmp_enabled` is true AND either `snmp_source_restricted` is false or `snmp_community_string_strength` is 'default' or 'weak'. An accessible SNMP agent allows adversaries to dump the MIB (T1602.001 - SNMP MIB Dump), discovering interface configurations, routing tables, and connected device information (T1016). Default community strings ('public', 'private') require no credential brute-forcing. Rated low criticality (score 2) but enables significant reconnaissance.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether an SNMP daemon is running on the load balancer host and which interfaces it is listening on.
how_to_obtain.command: systemctl status snmpd 2>/dev/null; ps aux | grep -i snmp; ss -ulnp | grep ':161\|:162'; netstat -ulnp 2>/dev/null | grep ':161'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active snmpd process or UDP port 161 in LISTEN state confirms SNMP is enabled. No process or closed port indicates SNMP is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the SNMP daemon configuration for enabled status, listening interfaces, community string values, and source restrictions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: agentAddress binding to 0.0.0.0 with rocommunity 'public' or 'private' confirms SNMP is enabled with weak, unrestricted community strings. Binding to 127.0.0.1 only or absent config indicates SNMP is disabled or localhost-only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt an SNMP walk against the load balancer from an external or internal test host to confirm whether SNMP responds and whether the default community string is accepted.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Successful OID responses confirm SNMP is enabled and reachable with default community strings. 'Timeout' or 'No response' confirms SNMP is disabled or blocked.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud load balancers, check whether SNMP is listed as an enabled protocol or management feature in the load balancer service configuration via the provider API.
how_to_obtain.command: aws elbv2 describe-load-balancer-attributes --load-balancer-arn <arn> --query 'Attributes[?Key==`routing.http.drop_invalid_header_fields.enabled`]'; az network lb show --name <lb-name> --resource-group <rg> --query 'sku'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cloud-managed load balancers (ALB, NLB, Azure LB) do not expose SNMP natively; if a software load balancer VM is in use, the host-level check above is authoritative.

option_description: Controls whether SNMP access to the load balancer is limited to a defined set of trusted source IP addresses (e.g., dedicated monitoring servers), rather than accepting SNMP queries from any host on the network. When restricted, only explicitly listed IP ranges can poll or interact with the SNMP agent.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags 'unrestricted_icmp_and_diagnostic_protocols' when snmp_enabled is true and snmp_source_restricted is not set. Without source IP restrictions, any host on the network—including a compromised internal system—can query SNMP MIB data, enabling network topology discovery (T1602.001 SNMP MIB Dump, T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery) and potentially exploiting weak community strings. Restricting source IPs significantly limits the blast radius of SNMP exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based load balancers (e.g., HAProxy with SNMP via net-snmp), inspect the snmpd configuration for rocommunity or rouser directives with source IP constraints.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as 'rocommunity <string> <source-IP-or-CIDR>' indicating restricted sources, or absence of source IP indicating unrestricted access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For F5 BIG-IP load balancers, use tmsh to list SNMP allowed addresses configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of allowed-addresses entries containing specific IP addresses or CIDR ranges. An empty list or wildcard (0.0.0.0/0) indicates unrestricted access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On F5 BIG-IP, navigate to the SNMP configuration panel to review allowed source addresses.
how_to_obtain.navigation: System > SNMP > Agent > Configuration > Client Allow List
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A populated list of specific IP addresses or subnets permitted to query SNMP. An empty allow-list or wildcard entry indicates unrestricted access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From an IP address that should NOT be allowed (e.g., a workstation outside the monitoring subnet), attempt an SNMP walk against the load balancer management IP to verify whether source restrictions are enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 'Timeout' or 'No response' result from unauthorized source IPs confirms source restriction is in place. A successful MIB response from an untrusted IP confirms the control is absent.

typical_values: true (SNMP ACL or allowed-addresses list is populated with specific monitoring server IPs)
false (SNMP accepts queries from any source, or no ACL is configured)

option_description: Represents an assessment of the SNMP community string configured on the load balancer. The possible values reflect the security quality of the string: 'default' indicates the well-known vendor defaults ('public' for read, 'private' for write) are in use; 'weak' indicates a short or easily guessable string; 'strong' indicates a long, randomly generated string; and 'none' indicates SNMP is fully disabled.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'unrestricted_icmp_and_diagnostic_protocols' when snmp_enabled is true and snmp_community_string_strength is either 'default' or 'weak'. Default community strings like 'public' are universally known and trivially exploited—any attacker can query MIB data (T1602.001 SNMP MIB Dump) to enumerate network configuration and system details (T1016). Weak strings offer marginal improvement but remain guessable under brute-force. Only 'strong' or 'none' avoid this policy violation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based systems using net-snmp, inspect the snmpd configuration file for community string definitions and assess their complexity.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines revealing the community string value. Compare against known defaults ('public', 'private') and assess length/complexity. A string of 16+ random alphanumeric characters is considered strong.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For F5 BIG-IP, use tmsh to display the configured SNMP communities and their access levels.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output listing community names and their access types (read-only/read-write). Community names of 'public' or 'private' confirm default strings; short, dictionary-word strings indicate weakness.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt SNMP queries using well-known default community strings from an authorized test host to verify whether the load balancer responds to default strings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A successful SNMP response to 'public' or 'private' community strings confirms default strings are in use. Timeout or authentication failure for both strings indicates defaults have been changed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On NGINX Plus with SNMP integration or on commercial load balancers such as Citrix ADC (NetScaler), review SNMP community configuration in the management console.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Citrix ADC: System > SNMP > Community Strings; or NGINX Plus admin dashboard under SNMP settings if applicable.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Displayed community string names. Presence of 'public' or 'private' confirms default configuration. Absence of SNMP communities or presence of opaque strings suggests strong or disabled configuration.

typical_values: default (community string is 'public' or 'private'; most common in legacy or out-of-box deployments)
weak (short, guessable string such as a company name or simple word; common in environments with informal change management)
strong (16+ character randomly generated string; found in security-hardened or compliance-driven deployments)
none (SNMP agent is fully disabled; recommended when SNMP monitoring is not required)
